beats.say: Here's the fairest case against GEICO's moat. One. Direct selling isn't new any more. Rivals have had decades to build their own direct channels. Two. A low cost moat must be earned again every single year. It isn't a patent. Three. The moat has now needed rescuing twice, and both times, the damage came from pricing. And four. The latest letter admits GEICO lost customers while it fixed its prices.

beats.say: So, here's our verdict. GEICO's moat is real. A cost advantage, built into how it sells. It has lasted nearly ninety years, but it has never protected GEICO from GEICO. Both near deaths were inside jobs. Pricing mistakes that no competitor could have caused. Whether today's GEICO is still the low cost winner, is being decided right now, in its price lists.

beats.say: In India, a lot of insurance is still sold through agents and bank branches, each taking a commission. So Goodwin's question still matters. When you study any company that claims to be the low cost player, in any industry, open a case file with three questions. One. Is the low cost built into how it sells, or is it just a discount? Two. Could rivals copy it, without hurting their own business? Three. Are its costs and reserves reported honestly? A wrong cost number is how GEICO nearly died.
